title: Zurich Completes Its Acquisition of ClearView on August 20, 2026: A$0.60 a Share in Cash, Three Life Insurance Brands and a Bigger Place in Australia's Advised Market
summary: Zurich Financial Services Australia acquired ClearView Wealth on August 20, 2026 through a scheme of arrangement at A$0.60 cash per share, about A$385 million, after approval from the ACCC, APRA, shareholders and the NSW Supreme Court, and will run Zurich, OnePath and ClearView as separate life insurance propositions.
description:
Zurich's purchase of ClearView, announced in February 2026 with completion expected by the end of the third quarter, has now been finished. Zurich Australia's customer notice states that Zurich Financial Services Australia Limited acquired ClearView Wealth Limited on August 20, 2026, through a members' scheme of arrangement. AdviserVoice reported the completion on August 21, and Insurance News Australia on August 24.

The terms are straightforward. ClearView shareholders received A$0.60 in cash for each share, which AdviserVoice puts at about A$385 million in total, and Insurance News Australia reported the same cash total. The scheme needed the approval of ClearView shareholders, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority and the Supreme Court of New South Wales. Dealroom reported that shareholders voted in favour on July 27, 2026 and that the court approved the scheme on July 30, with ClearView planning to lodge the court orders with ASIC on July 31, the date on which the scheme became legally effective, and to suspend its shares from trading from the close that day. It also reported that eligible holders would receive a fully franked special dividend of 5 cents per share on August 12. A scheme of arrangement is a court-supervised procedure under which, once the required majority of shareholders and the court agree, the buyer acquires all shares and the target is delisted.

The headline price at the outset was higher, and the difference is explained by that dividend. Yahoo Finance reported on February 25, 2026 that Zurich Australia would acquire ClearView Wealth for A$0.65 in cash per share, about A$415 million or US$295 million, with ClearView's directors unanimously recommending the deal and completion expected in the third quarter of 2026. The final cash scheme price of A$0.60 plus a 5-cent special dividend adds up to A$0.65, which is consistent with the original announcement. Yahoo Finance quoted Zurich chief executive Justin Delaney as saying the deal "brings together Zurich's strong capital foundation with ClearView's established in-market product and advice relationships", and ClearView chairman Geoff Black as saying Zurich "will be a great custodian to continue delivering ClearView's ClearChoice product."

ClearView is a listed group whose principal subsidiary is ClearView Life Assurance Limited, a life insurer that works with financial advisers. It reported A$436 million of in-force premium as of December 31, 2025, according to its 2025 annual report as cited by Insurance News Australia, a figure that had been A$413 million at June 30, 2025 in the announcement coverage. In-force premium is the annual premium on policies that are currently active, and it is the usual measure of the size of a life insurer's book. Insurance News Australia, citing IBISWorld, said Zurich holds about a 5.2% share of the Australian life insurance market on roughly $1.3 billion of revenue last year, making it the fourth-largest player, and that ClearView has a 3.9% in-force share of the $9.4 billion retail-advised life insurance market. The retail-advised segment covers policies sold through financial advisers, rather than directly to consumers or through group super funds.

What changes for customers is, for now, very little. Zurich's notice says existing Zurich, OnePath and ClearView policies, products, claims and services are unchanged, and that customers should manage their policies, contact customer service and make claims as they did before. It describes integration as something that will happen over time and be "carefully managed" to ensure continuity. Zurich, OnePath and ClearView will continue as distinct life insurance propositions, each designed for different customer and adviser needs, and ClearView Life Assurance Limited will keep operating under the ClearView brand. Advisers keep their existing support channels. AdviserVoice and Insurance News Australia reported that Zurich will keep ClearView's ClearChoice product open to new customers alongside its Zurich and OnePath Life offerings, and Zurich plans continued investment in technology and people across the three propositions. The notice adds that OnePath Life's life insurance business has transferred to Zurich as the final integration step in that earlier acquisition, without giving a date.

The history helps explain the strategy. Zurich entered the Australian life market in a major way in 2019 when it bought the OnePath life insurance business from ANZ, a transaction reported at A$2.85 billion that included a 20-year agreement for ANZ to distribute life insurance to its customers. Adding ClearView brings a book that is distributed through advisers, a channel in which ClearView was already established. Delaney said the deal creates "one of Australia's largest and fastest-growing life insurers" by combining Zurich's technology and balance sheet with ClearView's products and market relationships, and Head of Retail Tim Kane called it an exciting moment for the teams involved.

There are two caveats for readers. First, the sources give different totals for the deal depending on whether the 5-cent special dividend is counted: about A$385 million in cash for the scheme price, and about A$415 million including the dividend. Second, the market share figures come from an industry data provider as cited by a trade publication, and the sources do not give a combined Zurich and ClearView share. As with any large life insurance merger, the practical test will come over the next one to two years: whether claims handling stays consistent, how adviser relationships hold up, and whether ClearChoice remains competitive once Zurich's integration work begins.
source_name: Zurich Australia (August 2026), AdviserVoice (August 21, 2026), Insurance News (August 24, 2026), Yahoo Finance (February 25, 2026) and Dealroom (July 2026)

key_points: Zurich Financial Services Australia acquired ClearView Wealth Limited on August 20, 2026 through a members' scheme of arrangement; ClearView shareholders received A$0.60 in cash per share, about A$385 million in total, and left the ASX shortly after.

ClearView shareholders approved the scheme on July 27 and the Supreme Court of New South Wales approved it on July 30; AdviserVoice also lists approvals from the ACCC and APRA, and eligible holders received a fully franked special dividend of 5 cents per share on August 12.

The deal was announced on February 24-25, 2026 at A$0.65 a share in total, about A$415 million, with completion originally expected in the third quarter; the final cash scheme price of 60 cents plus the 5-cent dividend matches that headline figure.

ClearView reported A$436 million of in-force premium at December 31, 2025; Insurance News cites IBISWorld putting Zurich at about a 5.2% share of Australian life insurance and ClearView at 3.9% of the A$9.4 billion retail-advised market.

Existing policies are unchanged; Zurich, OnePath and ClearView continue as distinct propositions, ClearView Life Assurance Limited keeps operating under the ClearView brand, and Zurich says it will keep the ClearChoice product open to new customers.
why_it_matters: For policyholders and financial advisers, a takeover of a life insurer raises practical questions: will my policy change, who pays claims, and will the products I recommend still be available. Zurich says nothing changes immediately and that the brands continue, which is the main protection against disruption. For the market, the deal adds to the consolidation of Australia's advised life insurance sector, where a handful of groups now hold most of the business. The scale matters to competition, and it is why the competition regulator and APRA were among the approvals required.
